source.title: The Effect of Amino Acids on Wound Healing: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Arginine and Glutamine

extraction_metadata.scope_note: This is a secondary systematic review. The review’s own pooled syntheses and review-level findings are represented as review-level evidence. Findings from cited primary studies are not represented as if this review generated them. Bibliographic entries are not atomized. Model-extracted atoms remain needs_review because no independent human reviewer step is represented.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to evaluate the effect of arginine or glutamine supplementation on wound healing or parameters related to healing.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effect of supplementation of arginine or glutamine on wound healing or parameters related to healing.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors reported conducting the systematic review according to PRISMA and using a PICO characterization.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The following systematic review was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) statement. Furthermore, this review follows the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) characterization.

atoms.canonical_statement: The methods report searches for papers published before October 2020 in PubMed, American Physiological Society Publications, Taylor & Francis Online, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Google Scholar grey literature, plus reference checking.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The databases searched for relevant papers published before October 2020 were Pubmed, American Physiological Society Publications, Taylor & Francis Online, Web of Science, EMBASE, grey literature research with Google Scholar.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults older than 18 years with acute or chronic wounds who received arginine or glutamine; exclusions included non-human/non-in-vivo studies, participants younger than 18 years, diabetes when data were incomplete or original data absent, and languages other than English, Spanish, or French.

population.label: Adults older than 18 years, healthy or not, with acute or chronic wounds
exclusion_criteria: Diabetes when data incomplete or original data not presented
Language other than English, Spanish, or French

atoms.canonical_statement: The planned intervention was a diet supplemented with either arginine or glutamine for at least 5 days.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Diet supplemented with either arginine or glutamine for at least 5 days.

exposures.details: Dietary/enteral/parenteral regimens varied by included trial; study-selection section specified at least 5 days.

atoms.canonical_statement: The comparator was a control group treated with placebo or not treated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A control group, either treated with a placebo or not treated.

atoms.canonical_statement: Meta-analysis data were extracted from figures with WebPlotDigitizer and from article tables/text; changes in mean and standard deviation from baseline to final values were used, CRP units were converted as needed, and medians/quartiles were transformed to means/standard deviations.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane risk of bias tool across sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias domains.

The authors used Review Manager 5.4.1 with fixed-effects pooling, mean differences and odds ratios, and reported 95% confidence intervals; nitrogen balance and T-cell lymphocyte outcomes were stated to be converted to standardized mean differences because measurement scales differed.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The pooling of the data was conducted with the meta-analytic methodology, utilizing Cochrane Review Manager 5.4.1 (2020) for the different outcomes evaluated applying fixed effects... Nevertheless, for nitrogen balance and T-cell lymphocytes levels, data were converted into standardized mean difference (SMD) owing to the use of different measurement scales.

atoms.canonical_statement: Five arginine studies and 39 glutamine studies were included in the review/meta-analysis evidence base.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Five (5) and 39 studies on arginine and glutamine, respectively were included in the systematic review (Figures 4 and 5) (Tables 2 and 3).

atoms.canonical_statement: For arginine studies, the review reported low risk of bias for random sequence generation and allocation concealment in all studies, with less consistent blinding/other-bias assessments and high other-bias risk for Langkamp-Henken et al.

For glutamine studies, the review reported low risk of bias for random sequence generation in all studies; Goeters et al. and Xian-Li et al. had high risk for participant/personnel blinding, and more than half of studies had unclear/high risk in the other-bias domain.
In the pooled arginine analysis, hydroxyproline content favored arginine supplementation (mean difference 4.49, 95% CI 3.54 to 5.45; p<0.00001; I²=99%).

population.label: Participants in the Barbul and Nussbaum hydroxyproline comparisons shown in Figure 8

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 9 reports that glutamine supplementation increased nitrogen balance (standardized mean difference 0.39, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.58; p<0.0001; I²=91%).

population.label: Participants in 11 studies reporting nitrogen balance in Figure 9

atoms.canonical_statement: Across 21 studies involving 1042 participants, glutamine supplementation decreased length of hospital stay (mean difference -2.65 days, 95% CI -3.10 to -2.21; p<0.00001; I²=84%).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The effect of glutamine on LOS was reported by 21 studies involving 1042 participants. According to the meta-analysis, glutamine supplementation has shown to significantly decrease the days of hospitalization (MD: −2.65, 95% CI: −3.10, −2.21, p < 0.00001, Figure 10). Exhibiting a high heterogeneity among studies (I2 = 84%).

population.label: Participants in 21 studies reporting length of hospital stay

atoms.canonical_statement: Across 11 studies involving 696 participants, mortality was lower with glutamine supplementation (46/340 vs 89/356; odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.72; p=0.0004; I²=14%); the paper also reports an NNT of 10.
Five studies involving 210 participants showed a lower lactulose/mannitol ratio with glutamine supplementation (mean difference -0.01, 95% CI -0.02 to -0.01; p<0.00001; I²=97%).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Five studies involving 210 participants reported data on intestinal permeability, assessed by lactulose/mannitol ratio. L/M significantly decreased in those participants supplemented with glutamine (MD: −0.01, 95% CI: −0.02, −0.01, p < 0.00001, Figure 12). The heterogeneity given by I2 was 97%.

population.label: Participants in 5 studies reporting lactulose/mannitol ratio

atoms.canonical_statement: Eleven studies showed an overall reduction in C-reactive protein with glutamine supplementation (mean difference -1.10, 95% CI -1.26 to -0.93; p<0.00001; I²=82%).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Eleven studies reported the effect of glutamine supplementation on CRP levels... the overall effect showed the reduction of CRP levels after supplementation (MD: −1.10, 95% CI: −1.26, −0.93, p < 0.00001, Figure 13). The heterogeneity among studies was 82%.

population.label: Participants in 11 studies reporting C-reactive protein

atoms.canonical_statement: Five studies showed lower IL-6 levels with glutamine supplementation (mean difference -5.78, 95% CI -8.71 to -2.86; p=0.0001; I²=74%).
Four studies showed lower TNF-alpha levels with glutamine supplementation (mean difference -8.15, 95% CI -9.34 to -6.96; p<0.00001; I²=97%).
Figure 15 reports no statistically significant effect of glutamine supplementation on T-cell lymphocyte levels (standardized mean difference -0.16, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.01; p=0.07; I²=93%).

population.label: Participants represented in Figure 15 (315 experimental + 312 control)

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Figure 15 total: experimental 315, control 312; SMD -0.16 [-0.33, 0.01]; I²=93%.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that only five arginine studies were included, arginine effects on nitrogen balance and T-cell lymphocytes could not be assessed because too few studies reported them, sample sizes were relatively small, and high heterogeneity for both amino acids may have affected the meta-analysis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In the case of arginine, five studies were included in the meta-analysis... the studies had relatively small sample sizes... the high heterogeneity of the studies of both amino acids might have also affected the results of the meta-analysis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that arginine or glutamine supplementation can positively influence wound healing or healing-related parameters; arginine significantly affected hydroxyproline, glutamine significantly affected several pooled outcomes, and the T-cell lymphocyte result was not significant.
The research received no external funding.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Funding: This research received no external funding.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Conflicts of Interest: The authors declare that there are no conflict of interest.
